Article Title: PHP security flaws trigger global scramble; CERT-In flags critical vulnerabilities
Article Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used open-source scripting language that powers websites and web applications

Bengaluru:

It has been a difficult day for cybersecurity, with critical vulnerabilities in PHP triggering an urgent global patching effort, millions of reported hacking attempts, and precautionary shutdowns of some online services. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the scale of the incident was unusual, remarking at an event in Cologne in Germany that he had not seen anything like it “in a long, long time”.The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used open-source scripting language that powers websites and web applications. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely, disclose memory and potentially compromise affected systems.In its advisory issued on Wednesday, CERT-In said reports had confirmed large-scale exploitation in the wild and urged organisations and individuals using affected versions to apply security updates urgently.Google Cloud executives Chris Betz, chief information security officer, and Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said PHP and cybersecurity firm Wiz Research disclosed the two vulnerabilities after research that used multiple AI models to identify and help remediate them.Google Cloud said its own infrastructure was not vulnerable, but warned that customers running PHP applications on the platform could be exposed. It urged customers to update their applications to patched PHP versions and redeploy them. Google is also rolling out updated serverless base images for supported PHP runtimes, with automatic updates available for certain services and configurations.The scale of the response has extended beyond India. “In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. Companies and govt agencies in several countries temporarily restricted access to some online services as a precaution while they worked to secure vulnerable systems. Cloudflare’s blog said it successfully deployed mitigations for all its customers after the PHP vulnerabilities were leaked before their official disclosure date. The company observed attack traffic targeting customers and tracked how attackers modified their payloads to try to bypass its security. “Approximately 75% of all internet runs on PHP or some framework based on PHP including Wordpress, Drupal, Laravel, Joomla and these vulnerabilities impact the default configuration of the same. It allows a Threat Actor to achieve remote code execution trivially. This will allow bad actors to get access to your server,” said Anirudh Batra, threat researcher in Bengaluru-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK.
Article Summary: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the scale of the incident was unusual, remarking at an event in Cologne in Germany that he had not seen anything like it “in a long, long time”

Article Title: More adult nappies, more pet prams? What Japan and Korea’s numbers really say
Article Text:
Japan’s adult nappy production and South Korea’s pet-stroller sales reveal shifting demographics (AI-generated image)

When adult nappies overtook baby nappies

illustration

Pet strollers sell more than baby strollers

Two small objects offer a striking glimpse of demographic change in Japan and South Korea: a nappy and a pram. But the numbers behind them answer different questions.In Japan, more than 10 billion adult incontinence products were produced in 2025, against just over 7.1 billion baby nappies. That is a comparison by number of pieces. The adult count includes pads and liners as well as nappies and pants. It measures production, which is not necessarily the same as the number bought or used in Japan.South Korea’s 2025 finding looks similar at first: 61,418 tonnes of adult products supplied, compared with 54,001 tonnes of child products. The adult category overtook the child category by weight in 2024 and stayed ahead in 2025. But a heavier pile need not contain more nappies. Both Korean categories also include hygiene underpads.How different might the count be? One Japanese study calculated an average weight of 62.4g for an adult nappy and 32.1g for a baby nappy. Applying those weights to Korea’s supply gives the following, not an estimate of actual Korean sales:Those weights come from Japan and do not account for the mix of products in Korea’s supply.They cannot establish Korea’s actual piece count. They do show why the distinction matters: adult supply weighs about 14% more, yet could comprise fewer individual products. For adult products to lead by number, their average weight would have to be less than about 14% greater than the child average.The pram finding has a different boundary. On Gmarket, a South Korean online shopping marketplace, pet strollers accounted for 58% of pet and baby stroller sales by number through September 2024; baby strollers accounted for 42%. The result describes sales on Gmarket. It does not tell us which type sold more across every shop in South Korea, or how many homes have pets and children.The three figures are revealing when read precisely: Japan’s adult products lead by pieces produced; Korea’s adult products lead by weight supplied; and pet strollers led on Gmarket. Each captures part of a changing market. The unit and the source determine exactly what we can say about it.
Article Summary: In Japan, more than 10 billion adult incontinence products were produced in 2025, against just over 7.1 billion baby nappies. The adult category overtook the child category by weight in 2024 and stayed ahead in 2025. On Gmarket, a South Korean online shopping marketplace, pet strollers accounted for 58% of pet and baby stroller sales.

Article Title: Google changes its privacy policy: Your Gmail, Photos data may now be used for ads; what it means for you
Article Text:
Personal Intelligence is what links your Gmail to Google ads

Turning off personalised ads alone won’t stop Gmail data use

Google has reworked a long-standing promise about your inbox. Its updated privacy policy, effective October 16, now allows content from Gmail, Google Photos and Drive to shape the ads you see, as long as you have shared that data with other Google services. The change was first spotted by Android Authority.Until now, the policy carried a plain line saying Google does not show personalised ads based on your Drive, Gmail or Photos content. That line is still there, but it now ends with a qualifier: "unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads." In practice, this covers anyone who has turned on Personal Intelligence, the feature that lets Gemini and AI Mode in Search read from your personal apps.Google pitches Personal Intelligence as a convenience. Ask Search for dinner spots near your hotel, and it can pull the booking from Gmail and suggest restaurants close by. Once connected, that access stretches beyond AI Mode to Discover, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate and News. The Gemini app has no ads for now, but AI search results already carry sponsored content, and that is where the two meet.Google maintains the feature is entirely opt-in. In a statement, the company said ads will stay relevant to your query, the context of the response and your interests, and "will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library."Advertisers cannot see your emails or photos, and your name and email address are not shared with them. Ads built on sensitive categories such as health, religion, race or sexual orientation are still ruled out.Search, however, can still work with summaries and inferences drawn from your emails and photos, and those can feed into what you are shown. Switching off personalised ads in My Ad Center does not stop connected-app data from being used for AI personalisation either.To cut the link, open your Google Account and go to Data & privacy, then Personalisation settings. Select Manage Personalized Recommendations in Search Services, find Connected Content Apps under Additional Personal Intelligence, and disconnect Google Workspace and Google Photos. You can also switch off Personalized Recommendations altogether from the Search Services Personalization page.There is one more step. As Android Authority points out, disconnecting an app does not erase what Google has already stored in Search Services History, even if you delete the original email or photo. That has to be cleared separately from My Activity, or the old data stays tied to your account.
Article Summary: Google has updated its privacy policy to allow personalised ads based on Gmail, Google Photos and Drive content. The change, effective October 16, covers anyone who has turned on Personal Intelligence. Personal Intelligence is what links your Gmail to Google ads. Google maintains the feature is entirely opt-in.

Article Title: Airbnb announces a new ban that goes into effect starting November 20, tells hosts across the world that you cannot make guests complete ...
Article Text:
What Airbnb's new policy says

Airbnb hosts react to the new restrictions

Airbnb also restricts separate contracts

What the changes mean for cleaning fees

Airbnb is introducing new rules for hosts and guests. These new rules restrict the checkout tasks hosts can require guests to complete. The policy, which applies to bookings made on or after November 20, prohibits hosts from asking guests to do cleaning duties typically handled by professional cleaners. These include stripping beds, taking rubbish offsite and washing and putting away dishes.The company has also said hosts cannot bypass the restrictions by moving such instructions to other sections of their listings or providing printed checkout lists. The announcement has triggered criticism from some hosts, who argue that the changes limit their ability to protect their properties, while some travellers have welcomed the move amid longstanding complaints about cleaning fees and checkout chores.According to a WIRED report, Airbnb emailed hosts this week to inform them of the changes. The updated rules prohibit hosts from requiring guests to do tasks a cleaner would normally perform.Airbnb says hosts can still make reasonable demands, such as asking visitors to put dirty dishes in the washbasin. Other authorised directives might require guests to dispose of their trash in bear-proof containers or to save water in places with drought-related limitations.However, hosts cannot require guests to strip beds, wash and put away dishes or take rubbish offsite as a condition of checkout.Airbnb has also restricted attempts to circumvent the rules by placing cleaning instructions in a listing's “Requests” section. In an example shared in a Facebook group for hosts, a user claimed the platform prevented them from saving checkout instructions that included washing dishes, moving dirty towels to a laundry room and taking rubbish to a dumpster.The interface reportedly displayed a message stating, "Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task."Some property owners have criticised the announcement, saying the changes limit their ability to set expectations for guests and protect their homes.“As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces. The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official host forum.Another host, posting on Reddit, compared the platform’s approach to an abusive relationship, while some users talked about decluttering their rental kitchens or rethinking hosting altogether.Some hosts have also suggested raising rental prices or temporarily withdrawing listings to protest the changes.A third host took to a Facebook group to write, “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message. Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”But the policy changes go beyond cleaning instructions. Starting November 20, Airbnb will also ban hosts from forcing guests to sign separate contracts, with certain exceptions.These include situations involving local legal requirements, longer stays or access to optional amenities, such as golf cart rentals. Hosts must disclose applicable requirements in the designated section of their listings.Airbnb has also clarified that it does not enforce these contracts. Hosts who breach the new rules could receive warnings, have their listings removed or, in severe cases, be banned from the platform.The company already has ground rules requiring guests to treat properties responsibly, dispose of rubbish properly and avoid leaving dirty dishes that could become a health concern.The new policy comes amid longstanding complaints from travellers about paying cleaning fees and still being asked to complete checkout chores.Airbnb says cleaning fees cover standard turnover work, including laundry and vacuuming. Hosts cannot charge guests additional fees for failing to complete specific cleaning or checkout tasks, although they can still leave reviews based on cleanliness.The platform’s guest program, AirCover, also covers some types of guest-caused property damage, with eligible claims covered up to $3 million. The program can also cover other cleaning costs, such as removing smoke odours or cleaning up pet accidents.Some hosts say the restrictions could make it harder to keep their properties up to snuff, but travellers are embracing fewer chores, especially as cleaning fees are baked into the price of a reservation.The changes will therefore affect how hosts communicate checkout expectations, with Airbnb drawing a clearer distinction between reasonable requests and cleaning work that guests cannot be required to perform.
Article Summary: Airbnb is introducing new rules for hosts and guests. These new rules restrict the checkout tasks hosts can require guests to complete. The policy, which applies to bookings made on or after November 20, prohibits hosts from asking guests to do cleaning duties. These include stripping beds, taking rubbish offsite and washing and putting away dishes.

Article Title: Experts warn wave of AI-discovered flaws to trigger fresh disruptions in coming months
Article Text:
Weeklong disclosures and ‘fire drills’

Rapid breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) have begun unearthing a stream of hidden software bugs, and cybersecurity leaders warn that the discoveries are certain to trigger waves of disruption in the months ahead. The forecast follows a turbulent week where government agencies and public institutions across Europe, Asia and other regions took government and public portals offline to guard against newly surfaced vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that underpins a vast swath of the modern web. Citing multiple cybersecurity professionals, news agency Reuters reported that the episode is just the beginning.Matthew Prince, CEO of cloud and infrastructure giant Cloudflare, confirmed that he is tracking “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software.” He cautioned that the sector faces an intense operational stretch as algorithmic tools scour the foundational code of the internet for long-buried weak spots.“I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince was quoted as saying.The emergency scramble around PHP did not occur in isolation. According to VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity, it coincided with an already present cycle of security disclosures and infrastructure incidents across the tech landscape. Over the same seven-day window critical vulnerabilities were disclosed in Node.js (a popular alternative to PHP) as well as the streaming media platform Plex.Additionally, security breaches surfaced around AI gateway LiteLLM and modern application hosting platform Railway. Revelations emerged that Indian certifying authority eMudhra had relied on an extraordinarily weak cryptographic key, raising potential safety concerns for web users globally.“If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more. I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed,” Garrity noted.Modern software platforms rely on massive, sprawling codebases where overlooked flaws can linger for decades.In the past, discovering a complex vulnerability required specialised manual auditing. Engineering a working digital lockpick typically demanded weeks or months of meticulous reverse-engineering by highly skilled researchers. That delay granted security teams a vital buffer window to write, test, and quietly distribute defensive software patches.AI has upended that balance. Autonomous models can continuously audit millions of lines of code, flagging vulnerabilities in succession and synthesising functional exploit payloads in hours.
Article Summary: cybersecurity leaders warn that the discoveries are certain to trigger waves of disruption in the months ahead. The forecast follows a turbulent week where government agencies and public institutions across Europe, Asia and other regions took government and public portals offline to guard against newly surfaced vulnerabilities in PHP.

Article Title: US’ FCC bans more gadgets for China links, says these cameras and video transmitters run on ‘spy chip’
Article Text:
FCC blocks two gadgets over Huawei-linked ‘spy chip’

Why the FCC sees this Huawei camera chip as a surveillance risk

New FCC rule stops blacklisted chips from slipping into other brands’ devices

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has blocked a dashboard camera and a wireless video transmitter from the American market because they carry chips made by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon. The regulator calls the part a “foreign surveillance chip,” and neither device can now be marketed or sold in the US.This is the first time the agency has used a power it gave itself on October 13. The new rule lets it reject any gadget built around a chip from a company on its national security blacklist. FCC chairman Brendan Carr said such video devices “pose an obvious and unacceptable risk to the nation and our people.”The FCC has not named the brands or models of the two devices. It has, however, singled out HiSilicon’s Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC. This processor takes the raw feed from a camera sensor and turns it into a working home security camera, dashcam or similar device. The agency has not said whether this exact chip sits inside both blocked products.The agency’s case leans heavily on HiSilicon’s own marketing. The company pitches the Hi3516CV610 as a chip made for the surveillance market, with face detection algorithms built in.Its parent, Huawei, has sat on the FCC’s Covered List since March 2021. The list names companies and products Washington considers an unacceptable risk to US national security, and it extends to their subsidiaries and affiliates.The FCC has not said that either device sent data to Huawei. The block rests on who made the chip.The October 13 rule closes what the FCC describes as a component loophole. Earlier, a device assembled and branded by a company not on the list could still win approval, even if a blacklisted firm made the parts doing the actual computing. Now the FCC can block any device using a “logic-bearing hardware component” from a listed company, if the full device would have been barred had that company built it. In plain terms, that covers chips running digital logic at more than 9,000 cycles a second. Passive parts such as housings, wiring, resistors and plain battery cells are left out.The rule has limits. It applies only to new equipment applications, so products already approved can stay on sale. It also covers only companies named on the list, not the country-of-origin bans on foreign-made drones and routers.Online stores get new duties too. Marketplaces will have to show a device’s FCC ID at the point of sale, with deadlines of March 1 and June 1, 2027, depending on how much control a platform has over the product.The block adds to a busy year for Carr’s FCC. Foreign-made routers, power inverters and advanced robots, including robot vacuums, have all been pulled under the Covered List since March. Critics of those moves have asked whether such bans make users safer or mainly decide which manufacturers get to sell in the US. The FCC says it will keep enforcing its component rules aggressively.
Article Summary: FCC blocks a dashboard camera and a wireless video transmitter. Both carry chips made by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon. The regulator calls the part a ‘foreign surveillance chip,’ and neither device can now be marketed or sold in the US.

Article Title: PHP2Shell: Governments on high alert over critical website flaw; Wikipedia, hospitals, school portals go dark; what users should know
Article Text:
PHP2Shell: AI finds decade-old flaw in software behind 70% of websites; governments take sites offline

PHP is the hidden software behind most websites on the internet

The PHP2Shell flaw lets hackers take over a website without a password

AI found a flaw that had been hiding for over a decade

Most users on the internet can relax, but website owners need to update right away

A large chunk of the internet went offline on Wednesday, and most of it was switched off on purpose. Government websites in the Netherlands, Finland, France and Denmark, along with universities, hospitals and sites as big as Wikipedia, pulled systems down after two serious security flaws were found in PHP. Most people have never heard of PHP, but it is the software running behind roughly 70% of all websites, from news sites and online shops to personal blogs.The flaws, now nicknamed PHP2Shell, let a hacker take over the computer that runs a website without needing a password. They had been hiding in PHP's code for more than a decade, and it took artificial intelligence (AI) to find them. PHP's developers released a fix on October 21, but hackers moved within hours to attack websites that hadn't updated yet. Cyber security agencies in the US and the UK have told website owners to install the fix right away or take their sites offline until they can.The list of affected sites shows how far PHP reaches. The Dutch government's own cyber security agency shut its website as a precaution. Finland took several government online services offline, France's Interior Ministry put all its websites into maintenance mode, and Denmark shut its national school communication platform.In the Netherlands, the Port of Rotterdam, the national football association, several hospitals and the five largest political parties also took their sites down. The Internet Archive went offline briefly, and online forums 4chan and DeviantArt ran into trouble. Even Pokémon Home and Pokémon Champions were taken offline.Some world leaders got involved too. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi posted on X: "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight."The rush makes sense once you see how fast hackers moved. Cloudflare, a company that sits in front of millions of websites to protect them, saw thousands of hacking attempts even before the flaws were made public. CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X that this climbed to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions by the next morning.Think of a website as having two sides. The side you see is the page in your browser. The side you don't see is a computer, called a server, that builds that page every time you open it. It fetches the right text, images, prices or comments from a database and sends the finished page to your screen. PHP is the language that does this job for a huge share of the web.It has been around since the early 1990s, and it powers WordPress, the tool behind millions of blogs and business websites. It also runs Wikipedia, many government portals, and platforms like Drupal and Joomla that big organisations use to manage their websites. Web tracking firm W3Techs estimates PHP is used by about 69.3% of all websites whose underlying software it can identify.That is why a single flaw in PHP turned into a global problem. Tiffany Farriss, who heads the Drupal Association, told Reuters that any server running a version of PHP from the last 20 years would be vulnerable. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet," she said.PHP is also free and open source, which means anyone can use it. It is looked after by a small non-profit, the PHP Foundation, which has just 13 full-time and part-time engineers maintaining software that much of the internet depends on.Normally, to change a website or access its stored data, you need an administrator login. PHP2Shell skips that step entirely.The two flaws, officially tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are both rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity. In simple terms, a hacker can send a website a carefully crafted request that makes PHP run out of memory and stop halfway through its work. That leaves behind some leftover data in the server. The hacker then sends a second request that makes PHP use that leftover data as if it were normal, and that opens the door to running their own commands on the server.Once inside, a hacker can change what a website shows, plant malicious software that infects visitors, or steal what the server stores. That can include usernames and passwords, digital keys that connect the site to other services, and databases with personal information. A second route even lets hackers peek into the server's short-term memory, where they could catch passwords and login details of other people using the site at the same time.Wiz, one of the firms that found the flaws, showed working attacks on fresh WordPress, Drupal and Joomla websites. It also pointed out that the problem is in PHP itself, so even a basic website with nothing complicated on it can be at risk. Every version of PHP going back more than a decade is affected.The bugs were found by two security firms working separately. Calif says it spotted them on August 1 with the help of an AI model, which OpenAI says was its GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz found them on August 19 using its own AI tool along with Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.What stands out is that the flaws were not new. PHP's own developers had considered a possible attack along these lines in 2024, but nobody could work out how to make it happen. According to Wiz, turning these bugs into a real attack required so many complex steps that it was at the edge of what human experts could manage. With AI, a single researcher did in a week what would earlier have taken a top team months.The plan was to keep the flaws secret until October 22, giving website companies time to prepare fixes quietly. That plan fell apart when details leaked on online forums and social media on Tuesday. PHP rushed its fix out nearly a day early. Amazon later said its systems saw a hacking attempt on October 17, four days before the public announcement, and nobody yet knows how that attacker found out.OpenAI said in a blog post that the episode shows how AI can uncover security flaws, but also how it can help attackers "rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits." The same kind of AI that found the bug can help hackers study the fix and build an attack in very little time. That is why the window between a fix coming out and attacks starting has shrunk from days to minutes.If you only browse the web, there isn't much you need to do. The flaw targets the servers that run websites, not your phone or laptop. Still, a hacked website can be used to spread malware or steal data, so stay alert for a few weeks. If a service you use asks you to change your password, do it through the official app or website. Be careful with emails or messages about the PHP flaw that ask you to click links or share details, as scammers often use big news like this as bait.If you run a website, even a small blog, check whether it uses PHP. Sites built on Squarespace or Wix are safe, as those platforms don't use PHP. Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, says websites it hosts directly, along with Tumblr, are safe. If you installed WordPress yourself or use a hosting company like GoDaddy, Bluehost or Hostinger, contact your provider to find out when the fix will reach your site.The fixed versions of PHP are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Websites running PHP 8.1 or older won't get a fix at all, because those versions are no longer supported, so they need to move to a newer version. If your site stores customer details or takes payments and you can't confirm it has been fixed, taking it offline for a few hours is the safer choice. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre has also asked organisations that couldn't update quickly to check whether hackers have already left a hidden way back into their systems.Small websites run by individuals and small businesses are the most at risk, since they often lack a technical team and depend on their hosting company to apply fixes.Sigi Goode, a professor of information systems at the Australian National University, told The Guardian where the real danger lies. "The bigger concern is the websites that are not down today," he said. The websites that went dark on Wednesday were the ones taking the threat seriously. The ones still online without the fix are what hackers will be hunting for in the weeks ahead.
Article Summary: Government websites in the Netherlands, Finland, France and Denmark, along with universities, hospitals and sites as big as Wikipedia, pulled systems down. The flaws, now nicknamed PHP2Shell, let a hacker take over the computer that runs a website without needing a password. They had been hiding in PHP's code for more than a decade, and it took artificial intelligence (AI) to find them.

Article Title: Angry protestors 'interrupt' Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's event in Berlin, shout: 'What about technology found in Russian drones, those were ...'
Article Text:
Jensen Huang.

Nvidia CEO on 'Berlin protests'

Nvidia chips 'found' in Russian drones

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s keynote address at the company’s GTC conference in Berlin was interrupted by protestors on Wednesday morning. Minutes into the keynote, hecklers stood on chairs in the auditorium displaying a Greenpeace banner reading, "Nvidia, clean up your dirty business!" While the disruption was largely missed by the official livestream, attendee footage posted to Twitter captured demonstrators pressing Huang directly."Jensen, what about the technology that was found in Russian drones? Those were Nvidia chips. What are you doing about that?" one demonstrator shouted across the hall. "What are you doing about that? What are you doing about the environmental destruction?" The demonstration occurred during Nvidia’s three-day GTC Berlin event, running from October 20–22, which features developer sessions, executive panels, and industry talks alongside Huang’s opening address.The Nvidia CEO too made a small mention of the protests on stage, jokingly, he said, "All important issues, but let me get through my keynote." Huang remarked this before resuming the presentation.The outburst follows reports detailing the discovery of Nvidia components—specifically within Russia's S-71 "Monochrome" weapon, which relies on consumer-grade Jetson Orin modules for autonomous targeting—as well as in cruise missiles deployed against Ukraine.Some reports in August identified an autonomous Russian AI drone powered by Jetson Orin hardware as the cause of three civilian deaths in Ukraine, marking the first documented case of its kind.A Russian Molniya drone allegedly carrying an Nvidia Jetson Orin module crashed and killed three civilians at a gas station in Zaporizhzhia in August after choosing its final target without a human pilot. A New York Times investigation cited Ukrainian air defense commanders, drone experts, and the forensic team that examined the wreckage, as source of their report.Nvidia confirmed to the New York Times that modules photographed in the recovered drones were Jetson Orin minicomputers, hardware that sells for a few hundred dollars. "Our Jetson Orin modules are consumer-grade products sold to students, developers, and startups for a wide range of beneficial applications," an Nvidia spokesperson reportedly told Tom's Hardware.The statement added, "They are not available in Russia and are not designed for military purposes. Pre-owned Jetsons are available through many reseller channels. Although we cannot track products after they are sold, if we determine that any customer is violating U.S. export controls, we will take appropriate action."
Article Summary: Protestors interrupted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's keynote address at GTC conference in Berlin. Demonstrators stood on chairs displaying a Greenpeace banner reading, "N Nvidia, clean up your dirty business!" The outburst follows reports detailing the discovery of Nvidia components in Russian drones and cruise missiles.

Article Title: Anthropic introduces Claude Duet AI agent app for professionals: Features, availability and more
Article Text:
Anthropic introduces Claude Duet AI agent app for professional

Claude Duet: What can the new AI agent do

Claude Duet supports thousands of business tools

Claude Duet availability and subscription details

Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet, a new AI-powered app designed to help professionals and small business owners manage their work with less manual effort. The app can monitor connected accounts, flag tasks that need attention, prepare reports and handle work in the background, even when users step away from their devices. Unlike a chatbot that waits for instructions, Claude Duet can proactively alert users about important updates and help complete tasks across different apps. The research preview is now open through a waitlist for users in the US with Claude Pro and Max subscriptions, with access available on iOS, Android and the web.“We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track,” Anthropic said.According to the company, Claude Duet is designed to help users manage busy schedules and prioritise important work. Each morning, it can send a short summary of key items across connected apps. It then checks those accounts every few hours and sends notifications when something needs attention.Users can also assign tasks, ranging from scheduling meetings and drafting emails to building dashboards, preparing financial forecasts and developing web apps.The app is built around Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 model and is designed to decide which tasks need immediate attention and when it should ask users for guidance.One of the key features of Claude Duet is its ability to continue working when users are away from their phones or computers. The app uses a virtual machine with its own browser to carry out tasks in the background. Users can send instructions through text or voice in a single ongoing conversation and receive a notification when a task is complete or requires their review.Claude Duet also carries over existing memory, skills and connected apps from a user's Claude account, which Anthropic says should make setup easier.Anthropic says Claude Duet is designed to ask for permission before taking important actions on a user's behalf. The app can read messages, draft replies and prepare work independently. However, it must seek approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents or deleting anything.Some actions, such as trading securities or transferring money between accounts, are not allowed even with user approval.The company has also introduced additional safeguards to protect sensitive information. According to Anthropic, the system is designed to block requests to share highly sensitive details, such as credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, including health and personal financial details, can be shared only when users have explicitly instructed the app to do so.Claude Duet can connect with more than 6,000 connectors and plugins through the Claude Marketplace, allowing it to work with tools used by businesses. These integrations can help users find missed messages in Gmail and Slack, track unpaid invoices through QuickBooks or Stripe, prepare payroll in Gusto, draft job postings for LinkedIn and manage customer information in HubSpot.It can also help businesses create marketing campaigns using Canva and manage Shopify stores. Anthropic says support for a richer visual editor for Shopify storefronts is coming soon.Users can also make business purchases through Link, Stripe's digital wallet, and use Shop Pay for online checkout. Support for signing in to websites through saved 1Password logins is planned for a future update.Anthropic has opened a research preview of Claude Duet through a waitlist, starting with Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. The app is available as a standalone offering on iOS and Android, as well as through claude.ai.During the preview, Claude Duet shares the same usage limits as the user's existing Claude plan. Background checks and complex tasks can consume those limits more quickly than ordinary conversations.
Article Summary: Claude Duet is designed to help professionals and small business owners manage their work with less manual effort. The app can monitor connected accounts, flag tasks that need attention, prepare reports and handle work in the background. Unlike a chatbot that waits for instructions, Claude Duet can proactively alert users about important updates and help complete tasks.

Article Title: Decades-old flaw in PHP discovered by Google, OpenAI AI tools forces government and public websites to go offline globally
Article Text:
Representative image

Flaw impacting the ‘backbone of the web’

Flaw discovered through Artificial Intelligence

Government portals, municipal networks and public institutions across Europe and other regions went offline on Wednesday (October 21) after researchers disclosed critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a foundational programming language that powers a vast portion of the global web. The disclosures prompted emergency responses from IT teams worldwide, with operators taking critical servers offline as a defensive shield to prevent malicious intrusions before security updates could be deployed. Developers of the open-source PHP language published urgent security fixes for flaws that had remained buried inside the language’s codebase for years. Issuing an emergency advisory, the team stated that all site owners and server administrators are “encouraged to update immediately.”With tech security firms warning that malicious actors have already begun targeting unpatched setups, the disclosure triggered an immediate “race to exploit.” As fixes are now public, analysts warned that artificial intelligence (AI) tools could allow hackers to reverse-engineer the vulnerability with minimal effort.“Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale. With AI this is no longer a barrier,” noted cybersecurity firm Wiz, warning that AI-assisted attacks could lead to the mass compromise of unprotected web servers across the internet.Created in the early 1990s as “Personal Home Page,” PHP has evolved into one of the core backbones of modern internet infrastructure. When a user visits a webpage, servers running PHP assemble the text, media and code before serving it to the browser. According to web analytics tracker W3Techs, PHP underpins roughly 75% of all websites where the server-side language can be identified.“All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable. This issue impacts the majority of the Internet,” said Tiffany Farriss, interim chief executive of the Drupal Association.Due to this widespread footprint, national cyber agencies across Britain, Europe, Japan and Australia issued advisories directing web administrators to install updates immediately or take public-facing pages offline.The underlying security flaw sat hidden in the software codebase for over a decade. In a technical brief, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz revealed that human researchers would have found it extraordinarily complex to locate and exploit through conventional testing. Instead, the vulnerability was surfaced through advanced AI tooling:Wiz discovered the flaw using Wiz Atlas, its autonomous vulnerability discovery system, working alongside Google ’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz collaborated with the PHP core developer team, OpenAI and security firm Calif to verify the bug and confirm remediation patches.Early mitigation protocols were shared with cloud and infrastructure operators, including Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft, Automattic (operator of WordPress.com), Fastly, Akamai, Imperva and Vercel.
Article Summary: Vulnerabilities in the open-source PHP programming language have been disclosed. The language underpins 75% of all websites where the server-side language can be identified. The underlying security flaw sat hidden in the software codebase for over a decade. The disclosure triggered an immediate “race to exploit”
